title: Disasters That Changed the World · Episode 2
chapters: The Titanic: one night that changed the sea
Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded

units.t: Disasters That Changed the World. Episode two.
In this episode: Ireland's Great Hunger, 1845–1852, The Titanic: one night that changed the sea and Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded.
Part one. Ireland's Great Hunger, 1845–1852.
A microscopic organism destroyed one crop, and within a few years Ireland had lost a quarter of its people.
The blight was natural.
The scale of the disaster was not.
A crop and its killer.
By the 1840s Ireland had about eight and a half million people, many renting tiny plots from landlords.
Wheat, oats, cattle and butter were grown for rent and sale, but the poorest lived on potatoes.
An acre could feed a family for much of a year, and a labourer might eat several kilograms a day.
Many relied on one high-yielding but vulnerable variety, the ‘lumper’.
In 1845 Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like water mould probably from the Americas, arrived.
Leaves blackened and potatoes rotted in the ground.
Roughly a third to a half of the 1845 crop was lost, and 1846 was worse.
Other countries had blight too, but nowhere else was so large a share of people so dependent on the crop.
Relief, and its limits.
Prime Minister Robert Peel's government quietly bought American maize in 1845 to sell cheaply.
From 1846 Lord John Russell's government leaned on the idea that the state should not interfere with trade.
The starving were offered work on public projects such as roads, often for wages too low to buy food, and sometimes on roads that led nowhere.
In 1847 soup kitchens briefly fed around three million people a day, and they worked.
Yet they were wound down within months, and responsibility shifted to workhouses and local property taxes.
The Gregory clause denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre, forcing many to give up their homes to qualify.
Food leaving a hungry land.
One of the most painful facts of the famine is that grain, cattle and butter kept leaving Ireland while people starved.
Landlords needed rent, farmers sold crops to pay it, and armed guards sometimes escorted food convoys past hungry crowds.
Historians debate how much difference keeping that food would have made.
From 1847 more grain was coming in than going out, and the loss of the potato was too vast for exports alone to fill.
But most agree the deeper problem was choice, not supply.
A wealthy empire could have kept people alive and instead treated the crisis as a chance to reform Irish agriculture.
Charles Trevelyan, a senior Treasury official, came to symbolise that outlook.
Fever, eviction and death.
Hunger made people vulnerable, and disease did much of the killing.
Typhus, relapsing fever and dysentery swept through crowded workhouses, roadsides and cabins.
Scurvy appeared as diets collapsed.
Landlords, facing unpaid rents and rising local taxes, evicted hundreds of thousands of tenants, often tearing down cottages so families could not return.
Whole communities in the west, in counties such as Mayo, Galway and Cork, were devastated.
Around one million people died between 1845 and 1852, though exact numbers are uncertain because so many deaths went unrecorded.
Irish speakers called it An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger.
The worst year, 1847, became known as Black ’47, and mass graves from that time are still being identified.
The great scattering.
For many families the only hope was to leave.
Well over a million emigrated, mostly to Britain, the United States and Canada, some on overcrowded ‘coffin ships’.
At the quarantine station on Grosse Île in Canada, thousands died of typhus in 1847 alone.
Between 1848 and 1850 an assisted scheme brought more than four thousand Irish orphan girls to Sydney, Melbourne and Adelaide.
Ireland's population kept falling for decades and the island still holds fewer people than before the famine.
The Irish language declined, bitterness towards British rule hardened, and Irish communities abroad kept the memory alive.
In 1847 the Choctaw Nation, recently forced from their own lands, sent money to help, honoured today by a sculpture in County Cork.
Most historians see a natural disaster made far deadlier by poverty, a harsh land system and government decisions.
The key idea: Ireland's poorest depended almost entirely on one fragile potato crop, so when blight struck, there was nothing to fall back on.
Part two. The Titanic: one night that changed the sea.
On a calm, moonless night in April 1912, the largest ship afloat struck an iceberg and sank in under three hours.
The rules that keep ships safe today were written in its wake.
Big, luxurious, ‘unsinkable’.
RMS Titanic was built in Belfast by Harland and Wolff for the White Star Line and launched in 1911.
About 269 metres long, it was briefly the largest ship in the world.
White Star competed with Cunard on size and luxury, not speed.
First class had a swimming pool, a gymnasium and Turkish baths.
The hull was divided into sixteen watertight compartments, and the ship could float with any two flooded, or the first four.
A trade journal called such ships ‘practically unsinkable’, but it was not a central advertising slogan.
The boldest versions of the claim spread after the disaster.
Still, confidence in modern ships was real, and it contributed to too few lifeboats and ignored ice warnings.
Ice warnings.
Titanic left Southampton on 10 April 1912, called at Cherbourg and Queenstown, and headed for New York with over two thousand people aboard.
On 14 April the Marconi wireless operators received several warnings about ice ahead.
Not all reached the bridge, partly because the operators were busy sending passengers' private messages.
Captain Edward Smith altered course slightly but kept the ship at about 22 knots, close to its top speed, as was normal practice then.
The sea was flat calm with no moon, so no waves broke around the base of icebergs to reveal them.
The lookouts in the crow's nest had no binoculars.
Collision and sinking.
At about 11.
40 pm on 14 April, lookout Frederick Fleet spotted an iceberg dead ahead.
The officer on watch ordered a hard turn, but too late.
The iceberg scraped along the starboard side below the waterline, buckling plates and popping rivets along a long stretch of hull.
It was not one huge gash but a series of openings.
Water poured into the first five or six compartments, more than the design could survive.
Thomas Andrews, the ship's designer, who was aboard, told the captain the ship would sink.
As the bow went down, water spilled over the tops of the bulkheads from one compartment into the next.
At about 2.
20 am on 15 April, Titanic broke apart and sank.
Not enough boats.
Titanic carried twenty lifeboats with room for about 1,178 people.
That exceeded the outdated British rules, which were based on a ship's weight, but it covered only about half of the roughly 2,200 aboard.
Early boats left well under capacity.
More than 1,500 people died, many in water near minus two degrees.
Most first class passengers survived; around three quarters of third class did not.
The liner Carpathia, roughly 90 kilometres away, steamed through the ice and picked up around 700 survivors.
The Californian, much closer, had stopped for the night.
Its crew saw rockets but did not understand them, and its only wireless operator had gone to bed.
What Titanic changed.
Inquiries in the United States and Britain led to the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, known as SOLAS, agreed in London in 1914.
Ships had to carry lifeboat places for everyone aboard and hold lifeboat drills.
Wireless rooms on passenger ships were to be staffed around the clock, so no distress call went unheard.
The International Ice Patrol was created to track icebergs in the North Atlantic, and it still operates.
The wreck lay undiscovered until 1985, when a team led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel found it nearly four kilometres down, broken in two.
Its slow decay reminds us how a confident age learned humility the hard way.
The key idea: Titanic was built for size and comfort, and the claim that it was advertised as unsinkable is mostly a later exaggeration.
Part three. Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded.
In April 1986 a late night safety test went catastrophically wrong in Soviet Ukraine.
The disaster spread radiation across Europe and shook the Soviet Union to its core.
Test, flaw, explosion.
The Chernobyl plant stood in northern Soviet Ukraine, near the new town of Pripyat.
In the early hours of 26 April 1986, a night shift that had not prepared for it ran a test at reactor 4.
They wanted to know whether spinning turbines could keep cooling pumps running briefly if power failed.
Operators reduced the reactor's power and disabled several safety systems.
It became unstable, and they withdrew most of the control rods.
The Soviet RBMK design had dangerous features operators were not fully told about: if cooling water turned to steam, power could rise rather than fall.
When power surged, an operator hit the emergency shutdown, but a flaw in the rods briefly boosted the reaction.
Steam explosions blew apart the reactor, and burning graphite sent radioactive material high into the sky for days.
Firefighters and liquidators.
Firefighters raced to the plant within minutes and fought fires on the roof and around the reactor building.
Few understood how intense the radiation was, and some reportedly picked up chunks of graphite thrown from the core.
Two plant workers died on the night.
In the following weeks and months, around 28 more, mostly firefighters and staff, died from acute radiation sickness, despite treatment in a specialist Moscow hospital.
Helicopters dropped thousands of tonnes of sand, clay, lead and other materials onto the burning reactor to smother it.
Later, miners dug beneath it to install cooling, and huge numbers of workers known as liquidators carried out the cleanup.
Pripyat and the Swedish alarm.
On the day after the explosion, life in Pripyat continued almost as normal.
Children played outside and a wedding went ahead.
About 36 hours after the accident, residents were told to pack for a short evacuation.
Roughly 49,000 people boarded buses believing they would return within days.
They never did.
The zone was widened to about 30 kilometres, and more than 100,000 people were eventually moved.
Soviet authorities said almost nothing.
On 28 April, workers arriving at Sweden's Forsmark plant, more than 1,000 kilometres away, set off radiation alarms.
Swedish experts found nothing wrong at their plant and traced the particles to winds from the Soviet Union.
Under pressure, Soviet state media issued a short statement that evening acknowledging an accident.
Mikhail Gorbachev later suggested Chernobyl exposed the failings of the Soviet system.
Counting the cost.
Radioactive fallout drifted across Belarus, Ukraine and Russia and on to much of Europe, with rain bringing it down unevenly.
Farmers as far away as Wales and Scandinavia faced restrictions on sheep and reindeer for years.
The clearest health effect was a sharp rise in thyroid cancer among people who were children at the time, mainly because radioactive iodine got into milk from cows grazing on contaminated grass.
Thousands of cases were diagnosed, though most patients survived with treatment.
Estimates of eventual cancer deaths vary widely.
A major United Nations-led review in 2005 estimated up to about 4,000 deaths among the most heavily exposed groups, while some studies give much higher figures for Europe.
Many evacuees also suffered serious stress and upheaval, and the economic cost ran into many billions of dollars.
The zone today.
Within months, workers built a concrete shelter, the sarcophagus, over the shattered reactor.
It was rushed and began to deteriorate, so an international project slid an enormous arched steel structure, the New Safe Confinement, over it in 2016.
The last working reactor shut down in 2000.
Pripyat is now a ghost town, its apartment blocks crumbling.
With people gone, the exclusion zone has become an unexpected wildlife refuge for wolves, elk, deer and rare Przewalski's horses, though scientists still debate radiation's effects on animals.
In 2022 Russian troops occupied the site for several weeks during the invasion of Ukraine.
The key idea: A rushed safety test and a flawed reactor design combined to destroy reactor 4 on 26 April 1986.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why were so many Irish people exposed when the blight struck?
Answer. The poorest relied almost entirely on one potato crop.
Question two. What is the truth about the ‘unsinkable’ claim?
Answer. A trade journal used it and the boast grew.
Question three. What combined to cause the Chernobyl explosion?
Answer. A rushed test with safety systems off, and a flawed reactor design.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
